column2: On the authority of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him) that a man said to the Prophet (Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace): “Advise me.” He said: “Do not become angry.” The man repeated [his request] several times, and he said: “Do not become angry.” Reported by al-Bukhārī.
Rajulan (“a man”): perhaps Abū al-Dardāʾ. The view that he was Jāriyah ibn Qudāmah was challenged by Yaḥyā al-Qaṭṭān on the grounds that this Jāriyah was a Successor, not a Companion.
Awṣinī (“advise me”): [give me] brief advice comprising the qualities of goodness.
Lā taghḍab (“do not become angry”): do not expose yourself to what brings on anger, and do not do what it bids you.
Fa-raddada (“he repeated”): the man repeated his words “Advise me”, seeking something more beneficial than that, more far-reaching or more general.
Mirāran (“several times”): the narration of ʿUthmān ibn Abī Shaybah makes the number clear, for it reads: “Do not become angry, three times.”
Qāla (“he said”): the Prophet ﷺ said it to him the second and third times.
“Do not become angry”: its repetition [points] to its great and general benefit.
Treating every sick person with what suits his illness, if it is true that the Prophet ﷺ gave this man this particular advice
because he was quick to anger.

A warning against anger, for it gathers all evil, while guarding against it gathers all good. In this advice there is more bringing of benefit and warding off of harm than can be counted, for among the harms that result from anger are changes in the outward and inward state and an ugly effect on the tongue.

The outward change is in the change of colour, trembling of the limbs, actions coming out without order, and the distortion of one's features, so that if the angry person saw himself he would be ashamed of the ugliness of his appearance. The inward change is worse, because it breeds rancour and envy in the heart

and the harbouring of all kinds of evil; indeed, the change in his outward state is the fruit of the change in his inner state. Its effect on the tongue is that it is let loose with insults and obscenity of which a sensible person is ashamed, and which the speaker regrets when the anger subsides. The effect of anger also shows in action, by striking or killing;

and if that is missed because the object of his anger flees, the angry person turns on himself, tearing his clothes and slapping his cheek; he may fall to the ground, he may faint, he may break the dishes, or strike someone who has no part in the matter.

The command to adopt character traits which, when a person takes them on and they become habitual for him, ward off anger when its causes arise, such as generosity and liberality, forbearance and modesty, humility and endurance, refraining from harm, forgiving and pardoning, restraining anger and evil, and similar beautiful traits.
